title: The Heart and Blood
keyIdea: Your heart is a muscle in your chest that pumps blood all the time. Each squeeze pushes blood out through tubes called blood vessels to every part of your body, from your head to your toes, and the blood comes back to the heart in other blood vessels. You can feel each squeeze as a heartbeat: put a hand on your chest or two fingers on your wrist. The heart beats faster when you run and slower when you sleep, but it never stops.

kid: Your heart is in your chest. It is a strong muscle, about as big as your fist.
The heart is a pump. It squeezes, then rests, then squeezes again. Each squeeze pushes blood out.
Blood moves in tubes called blood vessels. They go to every part of you: your head, arms, legs and toes. Then the blood comes back to the heart.
Put two fingers on your wrist, below your thumb. Can you feel a tap, tap, tap? That is your heartbeat. Run on the spot, then feel again. It is faster now!
adult: In England, Year 2 science asks children to describe the importance of exercise for humans, and Year 6 names the heart, blood vessels and blood as the circulatory system. This lesson gives the younger child the core picture: the heart is a muscle, it pumps blood through blood vessels to every part of the body, and you can feel it working.

Words to use: heart, muscle, pump, blood, blood vessels (tubes), heartbeat, pulse. Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins bring it back; at this age 'out in one tube, back in another' is enough. A child's heart at rest beats roughly 70 to 120 times a minute, more after exercise and fewer in sleep.

Common mistakes to listen for: thinking the heart stops or 'rests' at night; thinking blood only goes to the chest or the top half of the body; thinking the heart is shaped like a Valentine's heart or sits in the middle of the tummy; and thinking blood in veins is blue. Blood is always red. Veins only look blue through skin.

In the lab your child squeezes the heart, joins tubes from the heart to the head, arms, legs and tummy, finds the beat at the chest and wrist, compares sitting with running, and checks that the heart still beats during sleep.

familyTip: Find your pulses together: two fingers on the wrist below the thumb, or a hand flat on the left side of the chest. Count the beats while a sand timer or phone counts 10 seconds. Then do 20 star jumps and count again. Which number is bigger? Make a fist to show how big the heart is.

visual.caption: Explore the circulatory system: find the heart and the blood vessels that carry blood around the body.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: squeeze the heart, join blood vessels to each body part, feel the beat at chest and wrist, and compare sleep, sitting and running.

practice.hint: It squeezes again and again, like a pump.
practice.explain: The heart is a muscle that pumps blood. Your brain does the thinking and your tummy breaks up food.

practice.prompt: Blood moves through tubes. What are they called?
practice.hint: The tubes carry blood, so the name starts with blood.
practice.explain: Blood vessels are the tubes that carry blood to every part of the body and back to the heart.

practice.prompt: Where can you feel your heartbeat?
choices: on your wrist, below your thumb
practice.hint: Try two fingers on the inside of your wrist.
practice.explain: At the wrist a blood vessel is close to the skin, so you can feel each beat. Your chest works too.

practice.prompt: Sam counts {a} beats in 10 seconds. After running he counts {b} beats. How many more beats after running?
practice.hint: Take the smaller number away from the bigger one.
practice.explain: {b} − {a} = {=b-a}. That is {=b-a} more beats, because his heart beats faster after running.

practice.prompt: The heart squeezes {a} times, then {b} more times. How many squeezes is that?
practice.hint: Add the two numbers of squeezes together.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} squeezes. Each squeeze is one heartbeat.

pool.hint: It squeezes, like the muscles in your arm.
pool.explain: The heart is a muscle. Bones hold you up, and air goes into your lungs.

pool.prompt: You are fast asleep. What does your heart do?
choices: beats as fast as it can
pool.hint: Does your body still need blood at night?
pool.explain: The heart never stops. In sleep it beats more slowly, but it keeps pumping.

pool.prompt: Does blood go to your toes?
choices: yes, to every part of you
pool.hint: Think of the tubes going down your legs.
pool.explain: Blood vessels reach every part of the body, toes too, all the time.

choices: about as big as your fist
pool.hint: Make a fist and look at it.
pool.explain: Your heart is about the size of your own fist, and it grows as you grow.

pool.hint: Put your hand where you feel the thump.
pool.explain: The heart is in your chest, a little to the left, behind your ribs.

pool.prompt: After the blood goes out to your arm, what happens?
choices: it comes back to the heart
pool.hint: Think of the tubes going out and the tubes coming back.
pool.explain: Blood goes out in some blood vessels and comes back to the heart in others, round and round.

pool.prompt: Ava feels {a} beats. Then she feels {b} more beats. How many beats in all?
pool.hint: Start at the first number of beats and count on the extra ones.

pool.prompt: Which one makes your heart beat fastest?
pool.hint: Which one makes you puff and pant?
pool.explain: Running makes your muscles work hard, so the heart pumps faster. Sleeping is the slowest.

pool.prompt: Leo's heart beats {a} times in 10 seconds while he sleeps and {b} times while he runs. How many more when he runs?
pool.hint: Take the sleeping beats away from the running beats.
pool.explain: {b} − {a} = {=b-a}. His heart beats {=b-a} more times while he runs, because his muscles need more blood.
